meta.title: AI-based Classification of Simulated Cosmic Radiation Bit Upsets into the SRAMs of a Commercial-grade FPGA
meta.authorsHtml: Artur Kazak<sup>1,2</sup>, Stefan Popa<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Andrei Bertescu<sup>1</sup>, Mihai Ivanovici<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Commercial-grade SRAM-based FPGAs can be qualified for space applications. For instance, they can serve as radiation sensors by periodically scanning their SRAMs for bit upsets. However, existing implementations lose data when the upset rates exceed the telemetry buffer capacity, precisely during high-intensity events that are most relevant for analysis. We present an enhanced architecture that integrates on-chip neural-network-based classification with per-element telemetry aggregation. A lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) classifies every pair of detected bit upsets within each scan cycle, distinguishing singlecell from multiple-cell upsets without prior architecture-specific calibration. In synthetic experiments, the MLP achieves F1 scores between 0.92 and 0.97 on structured bitinterleaving physical layouts and up to 0.72 with perfect recall on a previously unseen layout. This aggregation reduces the buffer overflow occurrence. We compare our method with an offset-histogram method from the literature. The two classifiers exhibit nearly identical resource footprints, but only the MLP operates without calibration.

blocks.html: Semiconductor devices in low Earth orbit (LEO) are continuously exposed to ionizing radiation from galactic cosmic rays, solar energetic particles, and trapped radiation-belt particles. When an ionizing particle deposits sufficient energy in the sensitive volume of a Static RAM (SRAM) cell, the resulting charge collection can flip the stored bit value, without permanent device damage [1, 2]. This phenomenon is known as a single-event upset (SEU). In modern deep-submicron processes, the charge cloud may extend to physically adjacent cells, causing a multiple-cell upset (MCU) that simultaneously corrupts several bits [3]. Distinguishing MCUs from coincident independent singlecell upsets (SCUs) is operationally critical because MCUs can defeat Hamming error-correction codes (ECCs) designed to handle only single-bit errors within a logical word. In 28 nm FPGAs, the scale of the problem is substantial: irradiation of an AMD/Xilinx Virtex-7 device (also 28 nm) with 3 MeV electrons produced over 28 million SEUs in the configuration memory and 1.76 million in BRAM from a single exposure [4].

SRAM-based FPGAs offer an attractive platform for radiation monitoring because their on-chip memory resources (i.e., Block RAM - BRAM, look-up tables - LUTs, and configuration RAM - CRAM) are inherently sensitive to SEUs [5]. For example, the heavy-ion saturation cross-section of BRAM and CRAM cells from 28 nm AMD FPGAs reaches 7.94 × 10−9 cm2/bit and 1.43 × 10−8 cm2/bit, respectively [6]. This sensitivity enables the use of the FPGA as a radiation sensor by writing known patterns into BRAM blocks and periodically scanning and correcting the deviations, combining radiation detection with hardware parallelism at power levels compatible with nanosatellite-class missions. However, the susceptibility of the controlling logic must be decreased significantly.

Such a radiation sensor was implemented on an low-cost and low-power AMD Artix-7 A200T FPGA, using the same architecture and 28 nm planar CMOS process [7, 8]. The baseline system comprises 256 detection elements (DEs), each realized as a single 36 Kb BRAM primitive, scanned in parallel at 1 kHz using 10 MHz clock signals by logic with triple modular redundancy (TMR) for all the flip-flops. The logical coordinates (i.e., timestamp, DE index, address, and bitmap) of the detected bit upsets (BUs) are transmitted to the nanosatellite on-board computer (OBC) via a Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) as 80-bit packets. The total power consumption of the optimized baseline is 0.712 W. A hosting PCB implementation targeting a 3U CubeSat form factor has been developed for this platform [9].

This baseline architecture has two principal limitations. Firstly, each detected BU generates one 80-bit SPI packet. At a 1 MHz SPI clock, the link can transmit at most 12 packets per scan cycle. However, the OBC polls the sensor at intervals that can span to tens of minutes [10]. Thus, the 256-entry First In First Out (FIFO) must buffer data across many scan cycles. When the sustained upset rate exceeds this capacity (e.g. during passage through the South Atlantic Anomaly, intense solar particle events, or ground-based accelerator testing), the FIFO overflows and data is irreversibly lost. Secondly, the baseline performs no on-chip classification: all events are transmitted in raw form, leaving MCU/SCU discrimination to ground-based post-processing.

Statistical methods such as offset-histogram analysis [11, 12] achieve excellent accuracy (F1 > 0.99) on structured BRAM layouts by detecting repeatable offset patterns. This method is topology-invariant, i.e. it automatically discovers the relevant logic offset peaks without prior knowledge of the physical interleaving layout [13]. Every time the logical offset of two BU matches one of the peaks, it is considered that they were produced by the same MCU. This method requires an architecture-specific calibration phase: thousands of scans under controlled irradiation are needed to build the statistical model, and the resulting adjacency list is specific to the FPGA architecture. Until this process is complete, classification output is unavailable.

Recent surveys highlight the growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques (including on-board neural-network inference) in space missions, driven by the need for autonomous data reduction and real-time decisionmaking under strict size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) constraints [14, 15]. The proposed enhanced architecture addresses these limitations through 3 contributions: i) onchip classification with per-DE aggregation using either the offset-histogram technique or a multi-layer perceptron (MLP); ii) calibration-free operation via on-chip MLP without requiring prior beam-test data, which achieves an F1 score of 0.72 with a recall of 1.0 in synthetic experiments; and iii) comparison of classifiers in terms of the FPGA implementations. The on-chip classification reduces the required telemetry throughput and implicitly the FIFO overflow occurrence.

We emphasize that we only used synthetic data in this work and we did not test the platform’s operation under irradiation yet. There are two main reasons for this: i) since controlled irradiation setups are not easily accessible, this work is a prior feasibility study, and ii) we require a dataset with 100% correct labels, which is not a certainty for real irradiation experiments. Several detected BUs might originate from a single MCU or from two or more coincidental events. Other works also employ synthetic SEU data in which such events are modeled as simple BUs [16, 17]. By contrast, our method accounts for the fact that the physical layout of SRAMs typically does not match their logical organization. Even the AMD Soft Error Mitigation (SEM) core [18], a module used to scrub the CRAM of AMD FP- GAs able to detect up to two errors per frame and correct up to one, has error injection features for such synthetic methods. Nevertheless, the platform will be deployed in a future 3U CubeSat, planned for launch at the end of 2026. Therefore, if launch and operation succeed, we expect to retrieve real radiation patterns from LEO.

The enhanced architecture augments the baseline by inserting a scan-aggregation and classification pipeline between the detector array and the SPI output. The top-level block diagram of the design is depicted in Figure 1. The original 256 DEs are retained without modification. The priority encoder is replaced by a scan-aggregator Finite State Machine (FSM) module that feeds the classification and packet-formation logic.

blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: After each scan cycle completes, the scan aggregator iterates over the 256 DEs. For each DE with detected upsets, up to four BU coordinates (i.e. 11-bit address and 5-bit bit index) are read from the local BU buffer. If a single BU is present, it is classified as SCU without invoking the MLP. For k BUs, where 2 ≤k ≤4, all dispatched to the MLP cores. Pairwise classification results are then assembled into a connected-component graph: isolated vertices count as SCU events, connected components of size ≥2 as MCU clusters. A single 80-bit classified summary packet is emitted per active DE, containing the BU count, SCU and MCU counts, maximum cluster size, DE index, and scan timestamp. The data flows from the DE array through BU buffers into the scan aggregator, which performs feature extraction and dispatches pairs to two MLP cores sharing a common weight dual-port ROM (consuming one RAMB18E1 primitive). Classification results are clustered, formatted into packets, buffered in the FIFO, and transmitted to the OBC via SPI upon request.

The MLP-based classifier operates with pairs of BU coordinates from a single DE. An MLP was chosen over convolutional or tree-based alternatives for its sequential multiplyaccumulate datapath, which maps directly onto a single DSP48E1 slice per core with minimal control logic [19]. For each pair of bit upsets (i, j), eight input features are computed by combinational logic in the scan aggregator:
• f0–f3: the normalized logical address (ai, aj) and bitindex (bi, bj) of BU i and BU j;
• f4, f5: the normalized absolute address and bit offsets, also used by the offset-histogram method;
• f6, f7: the squared offsets f 2
network to learn distance-based decision boundaries.

Division is implemented as reciprocal multiplication using 3 DSP48E1 slices shared between cores. Hidden layers use ReLU activation. The output exploits sigmoid monotonicity (σ(z) > 0.5 ⇔z > 0), requiring only a sign check on the final accumulator.

blocks.alt: The MLP contains 833 parameters after batch-

blocks.html: normalization folding [20], which analytically absorbs the running statistics into the preceding linear layers. All weights are quantized to 16-bit signed fixed-point (Q8.8: 8 integer bits, 8 fractional bits) and stored in a single RAMB18E1 block. The inference is performed by a sequential multiply-accumulate (MAC) datapath mapped onto one DSP48E1 per core, yielding a latency of approximately 890 clock cycles per pair (i.e. 89 µs at 10 MHz). Two identical cores share the weight ROM and operate in parallel, reducing per-pair latency to approximately 445 cycles. The five used DSP48E1 slices are distributed as follows: one MAC unit per MLP core and three for feature normalization (address scaling, bit-index scaling, and squaring), shared between both cores.

Training data is generated synthetically by modeling the BRAM as a physical SRAM array of 288×128 cells. SEUs are pseudo-randomly generated considering a uniform spatial distribution and a Poisson temporal distribution with an average of λ = 2.0 SEUs/scan. Each such emulated SEU can affect either one (90% probability) or multiple adjacent cells (up to 4 with various contiguous shapes). The logical aspect ratio can be different than the physical one. Five representative bit-interleaving SRAM layouts (the first 4 are structured patterns) are used: 1) linear (bit-major),

2) address-interleaved, 3) address-major, 4) column-major, and 5) random. The first 2 physical-to-logic maps are depicted in Figure 2. This enables classifier training without access to the proprietary interleaving pattern [13].

The fundamental contrast between structured and random bit-interleaving layouts is illustrated in Figure 3. For the linear mapping (M1), the offset histogram exhibits a small number of sharply defined peaks corresponding to the deterministic physical-neighbor signatures. This is the basis for offset-histogram classification. Physically adjacent cells can be logically far apart. For the random permutation (M5), physically adjacent cells map to relatively uniformly distributed logical offsets, producing no detectable peaks and rendering statistical peak detection ineffective. This interleaving pattern is not practical, but it is included in this work as an extreme case.

blocks.html: Two 80-bit SPI packet formats are used in the enhanced design, distinguished by a single header bit that now serves as a format indicator. The legacy format transmits each BU as an individual packet, identical to the baseline. It contains the 11-bit address, 18-bit upset bitmap, 8-bit DE index, 16-bit scan timestamp, and several status flags. The classification format transmits a per-DE summary which includes the total BU count, MLP-classified SCU and MCU counts, and the maximum MCU cluster size, reducing the per-DE cost from up to six packets to exactly one.

In the MLP-based configuration, the classifier processes every upset pair on every scan cycle—the system operates exclusively in classification mode. The legacy format remains available for diagnostic purposes but is not activated during normal operation. Thus, normally no additional bandwidth is required.

FIFO overflow occurrence reduction is a direct consequence of per-DE aggregation rather than a separate feature: even at λ = 200 SEUs/scan (typical LEO orbital rates are λ ≪1 [21]), the maximum number of classified packets per scan equals the number of active DEs and never exceeds 256.

Three design configurations were taken through the full FPGA implementation flow using the AMD Vivado 2024.1 tool while targeting the AMD Artix-7 A200T device: the baseline (no classification), the offset-histogram classifier, and the MLP classifier. The synthesis strategy was Flow_AlternateRoutability with LUT combining disabled, necessary to achieve routing closure at >90% LUT utilization and 10 MHz internal clock signals. blocks.html: Adding on-chip classification to the baseline requires between 41 000 and 43 000 additional LUTs regardless of the classifier chosen. The dominant contributor is the BUbuffer logic replicated inside each of the 256 DE instances: each stores up to four 16-bit BU records together with combinational selection logic, accounting for approximately 85% of the LUT increment. Post-implementation, the net difference between the histogram and MLP classifiers is only 1 695 LUTs (+1.4%), with 5 additional DSP48E1 slices and 0.5 BRAM tiles for the MLP. Power consumption estimation is almost identical: 0.839 W vs. 0.836 W. All three configurations achieve timing closure at 10 MHz.

The offset-histogram method and the MLP classifier are compared across the five synthetic BRAM bit-interleaving layouts and the results are listed in Table 2. Classification accuracy was evaluated in MATLAB (offset-histogram) and PyTorch (MLP). Both classifiers were subsequently implemented on the FPGA. The five layouts model representative physical organizations: M1 (linear/bit-major), M2 (addressinterleaved), M3 (address-major), and M4 (column-major) are structured patterns that produce repeatable offset distributions, while M5 (random permutation) serves as an adversarial case with no detectable offset structure. We do not consider this last model practical in real devices.
The offset-histogram method achieves near-perfect F1 (0.996–0.997) on all four structured mappings. On M5, the method yields F1 = 0 because no significant offset peaks are detected.

blocks.html: The MLP achieves F1 of 0.922–0.974 on structured mappings, with Recall = 1.000 in all four cases: every MCU event is correctly identified. The modest precision losses (false-positive rate 2.3–6.0%) reflect the effect of asymmetric training loss weighting, which biases the classifier toward high recall at the expense of precision–an appropriate trade-off for space applications where an undetected MCU is more costly than a spurious alarm. On M5, the MLP attains F1 = 0.183 (Recall = 0.833), which, while modest, is the only non-zero result in this scenario.

In the cross-mapping experiment (training on M1–M3, testing on M4), the MLP achieves F1 = 0.722 with Recall = 1.000, demonstrating non-zero classification on synthetic benchmarks without prior architecture-specific data. This represents a practical scenario for initial deployment.

As shown in Table 1, both classifiers add near-identical overhead; since the hardware cost is effectively equivalent, the practical differentiator is operational: the histogram achieves higher accuracy but requires architecture-specific data, whereas the MLP provides non-zero accuracy from first power-on.

Both variants consume approximately 0.84 W, with the MLP cores and feature-extraction logic contributing only ≈5 mW combined; the design remains within the nanosatellite thermal budget [8]; for reference, a 3U CubeSat with body-mounted solar panels typically sustains 7–20,W average power [22].

For architecture-specific deployment, the MLP is re-trained on beam-test data collected from all 256 DEs, assuming the interleaving pattern is identical across all the BRAM primitives on all the devices belonging to an FPGA family. The updated Q8.8 weights are then embedded via bitstream reload with no RTL changes.

Radiation-induced bit flips in the MLP weight memory itself could affect classification accuracy. Artificially injected bit flips in certain weights of a LeNet-5 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) can dramatically affect its accuracy [16]. The authors conclude that for increased SEU rates, TMR for critical bits of critical layers and weight limiting represent good mitigation approaches. In our case, LUT utilization exceeds 90% in both classification variants, leaving limited headroom, especially for TMR. AMD’s BRAMs are dual-port. For future work, we could duplicate the weights ROM and use a custom scrubbing module with Hamming ECCs specifically for it. Bit flips in the CRAM could affect the correct operation of the platform. In the presented configurations, we employ the AMD SEM core to mitigate their effect.

Two on-chip SCU/MCU classification approaches (i.e. offset-histogram-based and MLP) have been separately implemented on the same Artix-7 A200T. The addition of either classifier reduces FIFO overflow and provides real-time SCU/MCU discrimination at near-identical hardware cost, making the selection an operational decision rather than a resource constraint. When architecture-specific beamtest data is available, the offset-histogram method delivers higher accuracy. If immediate deployment without prior calibration is required, the MLP provides calibration-free operation with F1 up to 0.72 on synthetic benchmarks.

Future work will focus on decreasing the susceptibility of the logic to bit flips, validating the system under real irradiation conditions, and investigating domain-adaptation techniques to improve cross-mapping generalization beyond the current synthetic F1 values on unseen layouts.
